title: Palm Trees
text:
This analysis uses the TidyTuesday dataset from March 18, 2025, which comes from PalmTraits 1.0, a global database of functional traits for palm species (family Arecaceae). Each row is one palm species. The columns describe its growth form, stem and leaf measurements, and fruit characteristics.
Palms come in very different sizes. Some have no visible stem at all, and others grow into tall canopy trees. The plot below compares the maximum recorded stem height of each species across the palm subfamilies. Because heights range from well under a meter to tens of meters, the x-axis uses a log scale.


Code
library(tidyverse)

palmtrees <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-03-18/palmtrees.csv')

title: Palm Trees
text:
Stem height by subfamily


Code
palmtrees |>
  filter(!is.na(max_stem_height_m), max_stem_height_m > 0, !is.na(palm_subfamily)) |>
  mutate(palm_subfamily = fct_reorder(palm_subfamily, max_stem_height_m, .fun = median)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = max_stem_height_m, y = palm_subfamily)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "#cfe3c4") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.25, size = 1) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum stem height of palm species, by subfamily",
    x = "Maximum stem height (meters, log scale)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: PalmTraits 1.0 (Kissling et al., 2019), via TidyTuesday"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Each dot is one species, and each box shows the middle 50% of species in that subfamily. Subfamilies are ordered by median height.

Sources

Original data: Kissling, W. D., Balslev, H., Baker, W. J., et al. (2019). PalmTraits 1.0, a species-level functional trait database of palms worldwide. Scientific Data, 6, 178. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0189-0
The data reached TidyTuesday through the palmtrees R package by Emil Hvitfeldt.

title: Coffee Ratings
text:
This analysis uses the TidyTuesday dataset from July 7, 2020. It contains reviews of coffee beans by trained graders at the Coffee Quality Institute. Each row is one rated batch of beans. Along with the bean’s origin, species, and processing method, the data records scores for attributes like aroma, flavor, and acidity. Those scores add up to a total “cup points” rating out of 100.
The plot below compares total cup points across countries of origin. I only included countries with at least 25 rated batches, so that each box is based on a reasonable number of ratings. I also removed one batch with a recorded score of 0.


Code
library(tidyverse)

coffee_ratings <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-07-07/coffee_ratings.csv')
